en: (First Part) This *Padyāvalī*, composed by connoisseurs (*rasika*), is a sea of waves of joy, its verses made beautiful by their connection with Mukunda.
This delightful work, which subdues all darkness, is being compiled in due order for the delight of those who take pleasure in the collection of compositions. //1//
The auspicious invocation at the beginning of the work:
Homage to the lotus-eyed one,
who finds delight in the playing of the flute.
To the one who wears a forest garland and who delights in drinking the nectar from the lips of Rādhā. // 2 //
Of someone.

Affectionate in her glances as she bows with devotion, rivaling the blue lotus, and brought by those devoted to meditative absorption to serve as the object of their contemplation for the attainment of the ultimate good—
she who bestows a state of aesthetic relish upon the eyes of Rādhā, that great singular treasury of loveliness.
May the eyes or the body of Hari bring about the pacification of the suffering of worldly existence for you. //3//
Of Śrī-Sāraṅga.
Those peacock feathers whose plumage was stained by the mud at the foot of Govardhana;
those pillows for the playful reclining of the cowherd women in the laps of Vṛndāvana;
and those fragrant with the scented water from the ichor of the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa—[all these were taken].
May those arms of the enemy of Kaṃsa grant you constant auspiciousness. //4//
Of Śubhāṅka:

In the evening, the names of the trysts for calling the entire herd of cows back— names that are like the syllables of a perfected mantra for forcibly stealing the hearts of groups of cowherd maidens— [resound].
May the sounds of the flute of the one who assumes the form of a playful cowherd—the destroyer of Madhu—bestow prosperity upon you from every side;
those sounds which joyfully attract the rows of deer, the connoisseurs of the essence of Vṛndāvana. //5//
By Umāpatidhara.
(SKM 1.57.3) Now, the majesty of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa: By his waters, dry land becomes the ocean; by a mere speck of dust, the ocean becomes a mountain.

Salutations to that Kṛṣṇa, who, by his mere will, brings mountains to the state of particles of clay, grass to the state of a thunderbolt, a diamond to the state of withered straw, fire to coolness, and snow to the state of flowing water— a man addicted to the wondrous play of effortless pastimes. //6//
Of someone.

Because of his affection, because of his vow to grant fearlessness, because of his dispelling of the suffering of the distressed, because of his magnanimity, because of his drying up of sins, and because of his leading [beings] to the state of unsurpassed bliss—
therefore, the Lord of Śrī alone is to be served by all the worlds; for these [qualities] are his witnesses.
And Prahlāda, Vibhīṣaṇa, Karirāj, Pāñcālya-Halya, and Dhruva. //7//
Of someone.
Now, the greatness of the devotee:
What was the conduct of the hunter? What was the age of Dhruva? What was the learning of the lordly elephant?
What indeed was the superior beauty of Kubjā? And what was that wealth of Sudāmā?
What was the lineage of Vidura? What was the prowess of Ugrasena, the lord of the Yādavas?
Mādhava is pleased by devotion alone, for he who loves devotion does not care for mere virtues. // 8 //
Of the illustrious Southerner.
What distinction can there be between improper and proper action toward the Blessed One? Let the yoga of devotion alone remain most firm.
The lord of poisons scatters venom, yet the moon pours forth thick nectar.
That Great Lord bears both of these without distinction. //9//
Of the venerable Śrī Viṣṇupurīpāda.
O Slayer of Madhu, if a person of discrimination takes to heart service to Your feet or abandons it,
then all that evil karma throughout the three worlds [is destroyed].
The uncreated is not created, and everything is created. //10//
Of those very [beings].

The arising of the mind is not extinguished by saffron robes, nor by rules regarding food and the like, nor by dwelling in the forest, nor by exposition, nor even by the burden of a sage’s vows; rather,
it is for one sporting on the banks of the daughter of Mount Kalinda that [the mind is stilled].
Even from a mere fraction of the undertaking of worshiping Govinda’s lotus feet. //11//
Of someone.
Enough, enough! This very utterance "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" is sufficient for living beings in the matter of dispelling their sins,
provided there is devotion to Mukunda that is thick with bliss.
The Goddess of Fortune of the empire of liberation rolls at his lotus feet. // 12 //
Of the glorious Omniscient One.
Even when worship is performed with various offerings, the heart of the devotee— who is a kinsman to the distressed— melts with happiness through love alone,
as long as there is hunger in the belly and a persistent thirst.
Surely food and drink are for your pleasure, are they not? //13//
By Śrī Rāmānandarāya: If it can be obtained from anywhere, let the mind be permeated by the aesthetic flavor of devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
In this regard, even the price for such greed—namely, a single birth—is not obtained even through the merits of ten million lifetimes. //14//
Of that very [person],
knowledge exists as it is weighed upon a scale, but love is not at all weighed upon a scale.
In this world, accomplishment alone has been weighed on the scale;
the name of Kṛṣṇa has not been weighed on a scale. //15//
Of the venerable feet of Śrī-Śrīdharasvāmin.
Now, as for the greatness of the Name:
it destroys all evil for the entire world by its mere utterance once.
Like a boat across the ocean of darkness, the name of Hari, the auspiciousness of the world, is victorious. //16//
Of the illustrious Lakṣmīdharas.
Having extracted the heart of the four Vedas, Hari clearly fashioned the word "Nārāyaṇa" with its four syllables. (Nāmakaumudī 1.2; CC 3.3.180)
Singing this very thing incessantly, we now purify ourselves; yet we know that it is nothing at all for the gratification of Hari. //17//
Of someone.
May these twice-born ones attain fearless self-sovereignty, cultivated through the path of yoga, sacred revelation, logical reasoning, and meditation in solitary forests, and thus become liberated;
but for us, [there is the joy] of the blooming blue lotuses within the hollows of the groves of Kadamba thickets.
May there be hundreds of thousands of births for those who take refuge in the name of the Lord whose splendor is dark like a row of bees. 18.
Of the venerable feet of Śrī Īśvarapurī.
It is a treasury of virtues, a crusher of the impurities of the Kali age, a purifier among purifiers,

and the provisions for the traveler seeking liberation who desires the immediate attainment of the supreme state; it is the sole place of rest for the words of the best of poets and the very life-breath of the righteous.
May the name of Kṛṣṇa, the seed of the tree of Dharma, prevail for your prosperity. //19//
Of someone.
Sins tremble; the greatness of delusion assumes total confusion; the virtuous Śrī Citragupta experiences anxiety as he perceives the night of [Yama’s] claws;
and Brahmā joyfully exerts himself in the rite of preparing the honey-offering (madhuparka).
Since Your name is desired by the Lord himself, what else could we say that is superior? 20.
Of someone.
Who is the Indra of the city of the departed,
and who could be his servant?
It is the name of Kṛṣṇa, the sole auspiciousness of the world.
If one accepts the throat as the sacred seat (pīṭha), //21//
Of the venerable Ānandācārya:

It is the polishing of the mirror of the mind, the extinguishing of the great forest fire of worldly existence, the bestowing of moonlight upon the white water-lily of spiritual welfare, and the life-breath of the bride of knowledge.
Victorious is the supreme congregational chanting of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which increases the ocean of bliss, at every step provides the taste of full nectar, and bathes the entire self. //22//
Of the illustrious Blessed Lord:
whatever sovereignty belongs to more than ten million cosmic eggs, or whatever consciousness there is, is but a fragment of His.
That splendor manifested as the name "Kṛṣṇa" is my goal, my means, and my very life. //23//
Of some.
The very name of Viṣṇu removes the impurity of men and generates merit;
it produces detachment from the enjoyments of the abodes of Brahmā and others, as well as devotion to the two glorious feet of the Guru;
and having burnt away the seed of delusion regarding death and birth, it bestows knowledge of the reality of Viṣṇu in this world.
Having established the Person in the Great Absolute Bliss-Consciousness, it has ceased. //24//
Of the venerable feet of Śrī Bhagavad Vyāsa.
Kṛṣṇa, whose form is the essence of consciousness, is the wish-fulfilling gem;
he is complete, pure, and eternally liberated.
Because name and the named are distinct. // 25 //
Of those very [beings],
this is the most sweet of the sweet, the auspiciousness of all auspicious things,
the true fruit of the creeper of all the Vedas, the very nature of consciousness.
O best of the Bhṛgus, even if chanted but once—whether with faith or even playfully—the name of Kṛṣṇa can deliver even an ordinary human being. (26)
For them alone:
this resolve for the sake of heaven merely causes the worlds to languish.
The longing for liberation makes a person a mere partaker of affliction;
the practice of yoga is utterly tasteless—what is the use of such exertions?
Having abandoned everything, O Kṛṣṇa, let my tongue cry out "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! //27//
Of someone.

Indeed, your stainless primordial state always abides everywhere; yet, even for a single moment, it did not sever even one small leaf from the tree of worldly existence. But, O Blessed One, your name, when placed upon the tip of the tongue for even an instant, [severs] everything.
It consumes the provisions along with their very roots; which of these two, then, should be cultivated? //28//
Of the venerable feet of Śrī-Śrīdharasvāmin.

It is the attraction of those whose minds are refined, the uprooting of misfortunes even for outcasts, easily accessible to the world including the unlearned, and the subduer of the glory of liberation;
it does not require initiation, nor ritual service, nor even the slightest preparatory practice.
This mantra, consisting of the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, bears fruit merely by touching the tongue. //29//
Of the illustrious Lakṣmīdharas.
They are to be examined, to be investigated,
and to be reflected upon again and again.
May your names be ours, just as wealth belongs to the miserly. //30//
Of Śrī Bhavānanda.
The power of all your own faculties has been manifoldly employed in the creation of names; time itself has been constrained to the task of remembering them.
O Blessed One, such is your compassion even for me.
Such ill fortune has arisen here; there is no mutual affection. //31//
Of the Blessed Lord: (CC 3.20.16) Now, regarding the chanting of the Name:
"Being lower even than a blade of grass..."
Like one who patiently endures the falling of fruit from a tree,
Hari should always be glorified by one who is free from pride and who bestows honor upon others.
32. Of that very [name]:
(CC 3.20.21) "Śrī-Rāma," "Janārdana," "Lord of the Worlds," "Nārāyaṇa," "Bliss," "Compassionate One," "Beloved of Kamalā," and "Kṛṣṇa."
O Lord, may You always keep me submerged in the surging waves of the great ocean of the nectar of Your glorious names, making me repeatedly faint and helpless with tears falling from my eyes. 33.
Of the illustrious Lakṣmīdharas.
O Śrī-Kānta, Kṛṣṇa, compassionate one, lotus-navelled one, beloved of liberation, Mukunda, slayer of Mura!
I shall place this rosary of names around my neck, which surpasses the beauty and charm of a necklace of pure pearls. //34//
To them alone:
O Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Mukunda, Vāmana, Vāsudeva, Teacher of the World, Matsya, Kūrma, Narasiṃha, Varāha, Rāghava, protect me!
O ocean of compassion, worshipped by the lords of sages such as the gods, dānavas, and Nārada;
O son of Devakī, grant me unwavering devotion to Your feet. //35//
To someone [He says]:
"O cowherd! O ocean of the waters of compassion! O Lord of the daughter of the ocean! O slayer of Kaṃsa! O You who have crossed to the further shore of mercy for the lordly elephant! O Mādhava!"
O Rāmānuja! O Teacher of the three worlds! O Lotus-eyed One! O Lord of the cowherd women! Protect me; I know nothing other than You. //36//
Of the illustrious Vaiṣṇava:
O Śrī Nārāyaṇa, lotus-eyed one; O Śrī Rāma, Lord of Sītā; O Govinda, Acyuta, Delight of Nanda, Mukunda, Joy, Dāmodara!
O Viṣṇu, O Rāghava, O Vāsudeva, O Nṛhari, O crest-jewel of the lords of gods, O Hari who acts as the helmsman for the ocean of worldly existence, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, salutations unto You! //37//
Of that very [person].
O Bhāṇḍīreśa, O ornament of the peacock-feather crown, O Lord whose limbs are smeared with excellent sandalwood paste;
O conqueror of the forest of Vṛndāvana, dark as a blossoming and intense blue lotus;
O beloved of the Yamunā, O son of Nanda, O You whose eyes are like a lotus of supreme bliss!
O Śrī Govinda, O Mukunda of beautiful form, gladden me, who am wretched! //38//
Of the venerable Gopālabhaṭṭas.
The Greatness of the Narratives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
Even the Upaniṣadic teachings are far removed from the nectar of the stories of Hari.
Wherein there are no tremors of the heart, tears, horripilation, and so forth. //39//
Of the venerable feet of Bhagavān Vyāsa.
O Lord, I do not pray for the enjoyment of divine bliss, nor do I desire even liberation.
May the nectars of Kṛṣṇa’s playful deeds enter my ears day after day. //40//
Of Śrī Kaviratna.
Oh, day after day it is not afflicted by the Kali age;
at every step it is as sweet as a stream of nectar, and day by day it is as cool as sandalwood and the moon.
The fame of the son of Yaśodā is sung. //41//
Of that very [person].
For us who are immersed in the great ocean of the nectar of the youthful pastimes of Nanda’s delight, what [else remains]?
With the salt-water of nirvāṇa. //42//
Of the venerable Yādavendrapurīpāda.
Some fortunate ones, sporting with great joy in the ocean of the nectar of your stories, perform [their duties].
The fourfold group is like grass. //43//
Of the venerable feet of Śrī-Śrīdharasvāmin.
Right there flows the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā;
right there the Godāvarī and the Sarasvatī;
all sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell right there.
Where there is an occasion for noble discourse concerning Acyuta. //44//
Of someone.

That splendor of enjoyment which belongs to those who lust after the earth, that splendor of liberation which dwells in the hearts of yogis, and that splendor of bliss which belongs to the crown of the lords of connoisseurs— [may it be yours].
May that indescribable playfulness of Mādhava protect me. //45//
Of the venerable Śaṅkara.
Now follows the meditation on Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
He possesses the luster of a full-blown blue lotus, a face like the moon, and is fond of the peacock-feather ornament;
he bears the Śrīvatsa mark, wears the noble Kaustubha gem, is clad in yellow garments, and is beautiful.

I worship Govinda, whose body is honored by the lotus-eyes of the gopīs, who is surrounded by hosts of cows and cowherds, who is intent on playing his sweet flute, and whose limbs are adorned with divine ornaments. //46//
Of the venerable Śāradā.
[KK 3.82; KṛṣṇaS 106 (p49fn), attributed to the *Mṛtyu-sañjaya-tantra*;
ibid. HBV 3.114 (*sāradā-tilake ca*); in the RKAD to the *Svāyambhuvāgama*.]
Wearing a left earring that rests upon his shoulder, with creeper-like eyebrows slightly raised and the petals of his tender lower lip somewhat contracted, he gazes with sidelong glances;
joyfully filling his flute with the sprout-like fingers of his trembling hand.
At its root, one should meditate upon the Deluder of the World, charmingly posed in the *tribhaṅga* stance upon the wish-fulfilling tree. //47//
Of a certain [person]:
with a bamboo flute placed beneath [the chin] and a *campaka* flower fashioned as a crest-ornament.
I constantly bow to the conqueror of Kaṃsa, who holds his left shoulder in a graceful curve. //48//
Of the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama,
whose lotus feet are crossed, who possesses the grace of the charming *tribhaṅgī* posture,
and whose mass of hair is loosened over his shoulders;

I approach the one who has the peacock feather as his crest-ornament, who has accepted the bamboo flute as his staff, whose enchantment is effortless, and who possesses a preeminent compassion. //49//
Of Śrī Nārada. Now, regarding affection for devotees (bhakta-vātsalya):
[He] did not accept the hand extended by the vigilant commander-in-chief.

Homage to the haste of the Blessed One as he mounted the king of birds— which was devoid of a palanquin or ornaments— having forgotten his inner apartments and his exquisite jeweled sandals, even as it trumpeted like a noble elephant. 50.
Of the illustrious Southerner;
his words regarding the protection of the illustrious Draupadī:
"Like the rising sun in the darkness for those sinking without a boat."

Like a boat for those who are thirsty, like a cloud with sweet rain, like a treasure for those who lack wealth, and like a skilled physician for those afflicted by intense suffering and disease— Śauri comes to bestow welfare upon us. 51.
Of the venerable feet of Vyāsa;
now, the majesty of his devotees:
Prahlāda, Nārada, Parāśara, Puṇḍarīka—
I bow down to these holy and most exalted devotees of the Supreme Lord: Vyāsa, Ambarīṣa, Śuka, Śaunaka, Bhīṣma, Dālbhya, Rukmāṅgada, Uddhava, Vibhīṣaṇa, Phālguna (Arjuna), and others. //52//
Of the illustrious Southerner.
Parīkṣit became the foremost in hearing of Śrī Viṣṇu, the son of Vyāsa (Śuka) in chanting His glories,
Prahlāda in remembering Him, Lakṣmī in worshiping His feet, Pṛthu in offering Him honor,
Akrūra in bowing down to Him, the Lord of Monkeys (Hanumān) in servitude, and Arjuna in friendship.
In the offering of their entire selves, Bali became [the recipient]; this was the supreme attainment for them. 53.
Salutations to them, whose sandals are expert in delivering those who have become mired in the thick mud of the ocean of worldly existence.
Upon hearing the pair of syllables "Kṛṣṇa," those whose thrill of bliss causes their mass of body hair to stand on end [are truly blessed]. //54//
Of Autkala.

O Earth, carry that very bull among men until the moon and sun cease to exist— he whose mind is stilled by the joy of remembering Hari, whose body is covered in horripilation, and whose eyes are filled with tears of bliss.
What is the use of those other burdens which are solely concerned with going to and returning from the abode of Yama? //55//
Of Śrī Sarvānanda:
Your devotee regards the lord of rivers as a mere mouthful of water, the sun as a firefly,
Mount Meru as a clod of earth, and what more— regards the lord of the earth as a servant.

One regards a heap of wish-fulfilling jewels as a mere fragment of stone, the wish-granting tree as a piece of wood, and cyclic existence as a pile of straw; what more need be said? One regards one's own body as a burden. //56//

The intellect of those whose vision is stained by the dust of Mīmāṃsā does not reach even toward the Lord Sarvajña; as for those whose minds are harsh with fallacious reasoning that portends pride, any talk of Hari is far beyond their reach.

Even though they know it, they do not experience the bliss of the Śruti without the company of those who dwell in Śrīraṅgam; for even if a heavy ladle serves up a most delicious flavor, the tongue will not touch it. //57//
Of the venerable Mādhava Sarasvatī:
some rely upon knowledge, while others rely upon ritual action.
But we are merely those who hold the foot-protectors for the servants of Hari. //58//
Of someone.
Now follows the humble speech of the devotees:
"By their affection, they cause the festival of the mouths of the virtuous to swell with their very names."
Alas! Your dark-blue abodes, like collyrium for the eyes, spread their splendor;
the Sāman hymns born from the flute adorn the parched throats of those whose minds are not yet satiated by desire.
O Lord, even the mere hope for such things no longer shines before us. 59.
Of the collector-general.

Today, with your blazing Sudarśana, which dispels the exhaustion of the gods, [you have rescued] him who was seized by the crocodile of the three profound torments in the waters of saṃsāra— where the weight of delusion is amassed— and who was crying out from within out of fear of the fierce states of existence.
O Hari, pull out the lordly elephant of my mind that is obstructed by the continuous stream of anxiety! 60.
Of the collector-general.

O friend of the refugeless multitude, alas, O moon of the moonlight of compassion! For me, who am sinking in the deep and powerful flood of existence— filled with various manifest afflictions and driven by the force of delusion— you remain far away.
Without delay, grant me once more the support of your hand. //61//
Dancing with its own branches shaken by the wind, singing with the humming of bees,
shedding tears in the form of drops of nectar, and bristling with horripilation through its sprouts— the tree acts as the collector of taxes for the king.
Even the *mākanda* tree faints at the mere remembrance of you in Vṛndāvana; tell me, O one as dear as life, how is it that even your name does not enter my heart? (62)
Of the venerable Īśvarapurīpāda:
[That power] which was [displayed] in the protection of Draupadī, and that which was [displayed] in the liberation of the lordly elephant;
O Hari, embodiment of compassion, when I am in distress, where has that haste of yours gone?
O Lord of the Yādavas, remembering your name, "The Friend of the Wretched," I have fallen [at your feet] and am filled with longing.
Yet, because of your affection for devotees, my heart trembles as soon as I hear of you. //64//
Of Śrī Jagannāthasena:
"O Blessed One, the four-faced Brahmā and others are Your panegyrists, while Bhava (Śiva) and others are Your devotees."
O Vāsudeva, if Śatamukha and the other gods are your servants, then who are we? //65//
Of Śrī Dhanañjaya:
"The supremely compassionate one is not intent on others, nor is the most pitiable one intent on me."
Having reflected thus, O Lord of the Yadus, do that which is appropriate for me, a wretched man, toward Hari. //66//
Of a certain person,
struck by hundreds of whips of the afflictions arising from existence, wandering amidst the wrong paths of the sense-faculties.
O Mādhava, let the horse of my mind be restrained by the tethering post of Your feet with the firm bond of devotion. //67//
O Lord, you have not been meditated upon by someone, nor have you been praised, nor have you been even slightly propitiated;
nor has devotion been offered to your lotus feet within the range of their other births.
Therefore, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, storehouse of compassion, because I have become a vessel for manifold sufferings and have reached such a state, please show mercy toward me, a wretched one. 68.
O Śrī Śaṅkara!
You are my refuge, O Lord Hari, O Murāri;
victory to you, O Madhusūdana, Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu!
O Lord of the World, protect, protect me, who am devoid of refuge and who causes an endless flood of impurities! //69//
Of someone.
O Murāri, at the beginning of the day; O Murāri, at the beginning of the night;
O Murāri, at midday; O Murāri, at midnight;
O Murāri, at the end of the day; O Murāri, at the end of the night.
You alone are our refuge; you alone are our refuge. //70//
Of the illustrious Southerner.
O son of Nanda,
out of compassion for me, your fallen servant in this perilous ocean of worldly existence, [take me] by Your lotus feet—
Contemplate it as being like dust that has settled. //71//
Of the Blessed Lord.
(CC 3.20.32) Now, as for the steadfastness of the devotees:
"We are neither poets nor logicians."
They have not reached the further shore of the Vedanta, nor do they ward off opponents; they are merely servants of the young goat of supreme deceit. //72//
Of the venerable Śrī Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācāryas.
Let people speak ill of us however they may; we do not concern ourselves with it, for we are utterly intoxicated by the wine of the nectar of Hari’s love.
Let us roll upon the ground, let us dance, let us enjoy ourselves. //73//
Regarding those very [categories]:
"I am not a Brahmin, nor a king, nor indeed a Vaiśya, nor a Śūdra; I am not a student, nor a householder, nor a forest-dweller, nor an ascetic."
But [I am] the servant of the servants of the servants at the lotus feet of the Lord of the Gopīs, who is the rising ocean of the nectar of all supreme bliss. //74//

May the inner splendor of the Blessed Lord— the essence of truth and bliss, free from the power of transformations— shine within the hearts of the fortunate who dwell in the fresh groves of the king of mountains. (CC 2.13.80)
May some cowherd, whose passion for the gopīs is well-known and who yearns for the forest of Vṛndāvana, and who is as beautiful as a great sapphire, sport repeatedly within our hearts. //75//
Let those devoted to poetry praise the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of the venerable Īśvarapurīpāda,
and let those established in the nectar of Brahman residing at the head of the Vedas [praise] that nectar.
We, however, take refuge in a certain [deity] who wears a crest-jewel of gunja berries and holds a flute. //76//
Of the venerable Śrī Yādavendra Purīpāda.
For those who know that certain supreme reality which transcends meditation,
let the Self, which is pure consciousness alone, abide within the hollow of their hearts;
but for us, it is the one naturally sweet, with a smiling lotus-face.
This Self is dark as a rain cloud, encircled by gold, and lotus-eyed. //77//
By the illustrious Kavi Ratna.
(BRS 3.2.28) He never seeks the station of a king, nor does he take delight in the position of Indra; he does not direct his mind toward the perfections of yoga, nor does he long for liberation.
At the edge of the forest on the Yamunā, where the clouds are like steady flashes of lightning, my mind runs only toward the pure Brahman bound by the vine-like arms of the cowherd girls. //78//
Of that very [person].
O Sandhyā-vandana, may there be welfare for you; O Bath, salutations to you;
O Devas and Pitṛs, I am not capable in the rite of libation—may you forgive me.
Sitting anywhere at all, [I offer this] to the enemy of Kaṃsa, the best of the Yādava clan.
Remembering this again and again, I destroy my sin; I consider that sufficient—what need have I for anything else? //79//
Of the venerable Śrī Mādhavendra Purī Pāda.
O Bhavānī, what does it matter to you whether he who has become a servant of Devakī’s son wanders upon some wrong path or even upon the right path?
Let the mind proceed as directed by destiny. //80//
Of someone.

Let those skilled in policy call me foolish; let the Vedic scholars repeatedly call me deluded; let my circle of kinsmen call me dull-witted; let my brothers, having cast aside their affection, call me inert of mind;
and let the wealthy men of discerning wit call me at will a great hypocrite.
The mind is not able to abandon even slightly its longing for the feet of Govinda. //81//
Of Śrī Mādhava.
The supreme form is indeed dark-complexioned;
the city is the excellent city of Mathurā;
and the age to be meditated upon is youth.
The very first is the supreme aesthetic flavor (rasa). //82//
May liberation shine forth before the eyes of the teacher of the Lord of the Raghus; may he long exercise sovereign rule here in the kingdom of Virāja.
I desire only the service of the Lord of the cowherd boys. //83//
Of the venerable Surottamācārya.
You grant either the sovereignty of the earth or absolute poverty; constant honor or humiliation;
residence in Vaikuṇṭha or dwelling in hell.
Alas, Vāsudeva! I have no other refuge but you. //84//
Of Śrīgarbhakavīndra.
May he grant me sovereign bliss, or may he bestow upon me even the threefold torment—
whether I am happy or even suffering.
May Keśava not release [me]. // 85 //
Of the venerable Kavirāja Miśra.
Now follows the longing prayer of the devotees:
May the drops of nectar flowing from the lotus feet of the Son of Nanda [fall upon us].
May the rivers incessantly gladden my heart with the abundance of supreme happiness. //86//
Of the venerable Karācāryas:
"In this place he grazed the calves; in this place our Lord played the flute."
Thus, as I speak with tears on the bank of the Yamunā, may the day pass away. //87//
Of Śrī Raghupati Upādhyāya; in the garden-grove of his studies,
where a yellow sash is draped across her hips.
May my heart be fixed upon the deity of the Kadamba tree, who delights in the sweet warbling of the flute. //88//
Of Śrī Govinda: his long eyes are deep red, he is delightful to the sight,
and he possesses a body as charming as ten million Kandarpas.
May He, the sovereign emperor of the citizens of the city of Vrindāṭavī, dwell today within the lotus of my heart. //89//
Of Śrī Bhavānanda:
the ripening of the wave of sweetness within the forest of the nectar of loveliness.
May the deceptive youth, the very heart of all compassions, manifest! //90//
May there be births for the venerable Śrī Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya in those places where you, O possessor of the sweet sound of the flute, reside.
You have come to be drunk from by my ears; what use have I for news of nirvāṇa? //91//
To them alone [is it] like the flavor of the lips of a young woman, like the fresh chatter of a girl to be heard,
and like the beauty of the splendor of an excellent bride to be seen.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, may my offering, my conduct, and my very form be proclaimed incessantly like the words of a message from a wife long separated from her husband; may they become my Name. 92.
Some had their eyes streaming with a flow of falling tears,
and their faces were accompanied by voices choked with sobs.
When will your body be covered with horripilation upon the utterance of your name? //93//
O Lord of the Universe, I desire neither wealth, nor followers, nor a beautiful woman, nor even poetic fame from the Blessed One.
In birth after birth, may there be unswerving devotion toward You, O Lord of lords. //94//
To him alone [belongs] Govardhana Hill, a fresh rain-cloud;
the daughter of Kalinda, a fresh blue lotus.
May the noble Tamāla tree of Vṛndāvana bring about the immediate end of the threefold suffering. //95//
Of the illustrious Gauḍīya [Kṛṣṇa]: his beautiful corners of the eyes, restless with the skillful charm of amorous passion,
and his cheeks radiant with the luster of shimmering shark-shaped earrings;
May that certain cowherd, eager for the rāsa dance and the playful movements of the multitude of city women who have come from Vraja, suddenly manifest within my mind. //96//
Of the venerable Śrī Mādhavendrapurīpāda.
Now, the longing of the devotees:
the Vedas are like mere straw.
What should we gather here now?
For long ago, the Supreme Brahman was already brought here by the eyes of the Ābhīra women. (97)
Of the venerable teacher Raghupati.
To whom am I now able to speak, or who can find conviction in this matter within the grove of the daughter of the Lord of Cows?
The Brahman is the protector, the supporter, and the pervader of the world. //98//
By him alone has the system of Kaṇabhuj been known; the science of logic (anvīkṣikī) has been mastered;
the Mīmāṃsā has been studied; the path of Sāṅkhya has been understood; and the mind has been directed toward Yoga.
Though the Vedāntas have been studied with zeal, a certain stream of shimmering sweetness—the flute of Nanda’s son—draws my heart away. //99//
Of the venerable Śrī Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya:
a certain wave of the sweetness of the nectar from the mouths of the immortals,
a unique artistry of the fine arts.
The continuous flow of Murāri’s flute-music agitates my mind. //100//
It is they alone [who say]:
"This certain thief Kṛṣṇa— who steals away the misdeeds of those who bow to him and who stole the life-breath of Pūtanā— is stealing my mind."
The thief of the bracelets and garments, the thief of the eyes and hearts of the young cowherd girls, [and the thief] of the sight of the virtuous people. //101//
For some, enough with talk of the triple heaven; what use is the glory of universal sovereignty?
Let even the splendor of liberation remain far away.
Within the heart of the clusters of groves on the banks of the daughter of Mount Kalinda, there is a splendor, dark as a fresh tamāla tree, that captivates the mind alone. //102//
Of Śrī Haridāsa:
it was gazed upon, approved,
and embraced by women with their passions.
We pay homage to the grove of Vṛndāvana, which is like a mass of emeralds. //103//
O you who delight in all branches of knowledge,
when shall I behold the child Nanda wearing a garland of *nīpa* flowers?
The protector of all sentient beings, whose forehead bears a shining tilaka. //104//
Of the venerable Śrī Mādhavendra Purīpāda:
When, repeatedly wandering in the forest of Vṛndāvana— purified by the touch of the daughter of the Sun— one contemplates the waves of the pastimes of the Lord of Gokula;
Speaking loudly with the streams of tears from my eyes, I shall eagerly provide a thick irrigation for the trees. //105//
In the hair-tuft of the Collector-General, which is difficult to ascend and possessed of splendor— though it bears the very footprints of the Goddesses of Fortune—
the Upanishads of women dance upon its firm surface.
That flute-born melody of the Enemy of Mura, possessing such sweetness, will suddenly ascend to the very pinnacle of our hearing. //106//
This was the residence of Samāhartṛ; here, it is said, was the house of Nanda; here occurred the breaking of Śakaṭa’s cart;
and here Dāmodara, though he was the one who severs all bonds, was bound by ropes.
Drinking thus the stream of nectar flowing from the mouths of the elders of Mathurā, with tears of joy streaming down, when shall I, blessed one, wander through the city of Madhupurī?
Possessing the delightful beauty of a blossoming peacock feather... (as quoted in BRS 1.3.40— found in the *Padyāvalī*, though not located in this edition).
When will Kṛṣṇa come within the range of my vision— his lotus-face resting upon his mother’s breast, moving the tips of his lotus-feet? (107)
Of someone;
or else, a lack of regard for liberation;
devotion is service to the Blessed One.
Liberation is the transcending of that state.
What fool, having attained servitude, would desire a position of power? (110)
I long for that [state] which severs the bond of worldly existence for those who are silent in the presence of Śrī Śiva; I do not long for mere liberation.
Where [the distinction] that "you are the master and I am the servant" is obliterated. //111//
To Śrī Hanumān:
Alas, O friend, my mind is filled with wonder upon remembering them.
Even those who possess discernment might still harbor craving for ultimate dissolution. //112//
To some [he said]:
"Who are you? You have arrived as liberation. From where, O lady, have you come here so unexpectedly?
By the remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O goddess, you have been brought to the state of my servant."
Stay far away, O slight offense; how could a base person act so toward me, lest the fragrance of you—who are like an ointment of sandalwood paste named after yourself—be lost upon me? (113)
Of someone [who thinks thus]:
"Now, regarding the true nature of the Blessed Lord’s dharma:
to perceive a stone in the worshipful Viṣṇu, the notion of a mere man in the gurus, and the idea of caste-identity in a Vaiṣṇava..."
He who perceives the water at the lotus feet of Viṣṇu or His devotees—which crush the impurities of the Kali age—as mere water;
he who perceives the name of Śrī Viṣṇu, the mantra that destroys all defilements, as a common word;
or he who regards Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, as equal to others—he is a denizen of hell. (114)
Of the illustrious Southerner.
The *tulasī* that has touched His feet destroys the sin of killing; the water from His feet destroys theft;

the food offerings (*naivedya*) destroy the evil of excessive drinking of liquor; and the presence of one whose mind is fixed on the Lord Śādhin destroys the sin born of adultery with the teacher’s wife. Likewise, the company of the Lord’s devotees destroys the sin arising from association with them.
This greatness of the Śālāgrāma stone Nṛsiṃha is truly extraordinary and transcendent. //115//
Of the Śrī-Āgama.
Now, the prayer for the offering of the *naivedya*:
"In the soft rice-offering of the twice-born women, and in the *vidūrānna* [millet] of the cows of Vraja..."

O Enemy of Mura, may that fragrance which was yours when You tasted the thick, flattened, and polished curd and milk of Your friend Yaśodā’s breast, and likewise the honey offered by the young women of Vraja, be present even now in this offering. 116.
Of Śrī Rāmānuja:
"O Enemy of Mura, that same love which You have for Vidura's offering, such as that which You have for what was offered by Kuntī,
that which is on the peak of Govardhana, and that which is in the *pṛthuka* grain upon the breast offered by Yaśodā..."
Just as you accepted the lower lip offered by Bhāradvāja and given by Śabarī,
so too do I offer that same [lip] here to you, who have been presented with food by the female ascetic.
To someone, milk was offered by Śyāmalā; molasses was bestowed by Kamalā;
sweetmeat balls were given by Bhadrā; and a sweet syrup was obtained from Sobhābhayā.
O Hari, since there is such satisfaction for you from this, please place a hundredfold greater delight in the beautiful offerings presented by me before you at Rādhā’s command.
Of the collector-general.
Now, the Glory of Śrī Mathurā:
O Mother Mathurā, you alone are surely blessed upon the surface of the earth;
may hundreds of sincere prostrations to you always be ours.
Alas! Having abandoned Vaikuṇṭha, which possesses most wonderful qualities, that lotus-eyed Lord Hari has descended out of longing for you. 119.
In this place, it is said, was the home of Nanda; here occurred the breaking of Śakaṭa’s cart;
and here Dāmodara, though he severs all bonds, was bound by ropes.
Drinking thus the stream of nectar flowing from the mouths of the elders of Mathurā, with tears of joy welling up, when shall I, blessed one, wander through the city of Madhupurī? 120.
Of the illustrious Kaviśekhara:
(BRS 1.3.40) Wherein even the lotus-born Brahmā, the primordial teacher of all, desired birth from a pillar in the form of a pillar.
Adorned with rows of feet shimmering like wheels, banners, and goads, that Mathurā, the capital of the King of Hari, shines resplendent today. //121//
Of someone.

It is the seed of the tree of liberation, the deliverer from the mass of misfortunes, the illuminating light of the essence of divine love, and the means of crossing over to the further shore that fulfills all desires;
for those who dwell therein, these two functions of the power of consciousness arise.
May that city of Mathurā crush your misfortunes and bestow prosperity upon you. //122//
Of the collector.
O Destroyer of Mura,
Your Lordship never bestows upon those who worship You that yoga of devotion which You, alas, now grant to me.
Your greatness, O Mathurā, is beyond the scope of words. //123//
Of that very [person].
Mathurā is in hearing, Mathurā is in sight,
Mathurā is in speech, and Mathurā is in the heart;
Mathurā is before us, and Mathurā is behind us.
Sweet, sweet is Mathurā; Mathurā! //124//
By Śrī Govinda Miśra.
Now, the salutation to Śrī Vṛndāṭavī:
Worship Hiraṇyagarbha.
I bow to you, Hara; I bow to you, the Supreme Brahman; but I bow to the forest of Vṛndāvana, wherein the bliss of Kṛṣṇa is established. //125//
Of someone.
Now follows the salutation to Śrī Nanda:
some [follow] the Śruti, others the Smṛti.
Let others who are afraid of worldly existence devote themselves to Bhārata; I, however, here salute Nanda, in whose courtyard dwells the Supreme Brahman. 126.
Of the preceptor of the Lord of the Raghus: (CC 2.19.96) He whose garment is as crimson as the bandhūka flower,
who has a beautiful beard, and whose eyes have been captivated by Mukunda.
I pay homage to Nanda, whose body is pot-bellied and whose complexion is as fair as sandalwood. //127//
Of the Collector;
now follows the salutation to Śrī-Yaśodā:
[to her] whose lotus-navel rests upon her lap.
I repeatedly pay homage to Yaśodā, who possesses the luster of a fresh cloud, whose garments are of variegated brilliance, and who brings constant joy to the world. //128//
Of the Collector-General; now, the childhood of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa,
with hands and feet that are exceedingly red.
I bow to Murāri, who lies on his back with a beautiful mark of yellow pigment upon his forehead, having forcibly overturned the cart. 129.
Of a certain [child],
whose eyes were half-open, who was drinking from one breast that was already drenched with freshly flowing milk, while wiping the other with his hand;
May the luster of Viṣṇu’s teeth—white as a vast expanse of milk droplets—protect you, as his face repeatedly breaks into smiles while he plays with a morsel of food held between his fingers. 130.
Of Śrī-Maṅgala:
[I praise him] whose restless eyes are drawn by the *phūtkṛti* (hissing sound) from the mouth of Gopeśvarī,
as he crawls along the earth on his two knees.
I worship that Child, whose dark-blue body is like a tamāla leaf, and whose lips are as sweet as the nectar of a fresh smile. //131//
By Śrī Raghunāthadāsa:
(BRK 5.1738) "Where is the face? Where are the eyes? Where is the nose? Where is the ear? Where is the crest?"—thus he was instructed.
There, the Lord delighted the assembly of cowherd women by placing his petal-like fingers upon this and that spot. //132//
Of the Emperor of Poets.
(BRK 5.1740) Now the limbs have been washed and the ointment applied.
O Kṛṣṇa, even now your body is covered in grey dust.
Of the Sarvabhauma Bhaṭṭācāryas:
(BRK 5.1742) O lady, [I see] a five-year-old child, exceedingly restless, running about with eyes clouded by disheveled hair.
Bow down to the one who delights Nanda, who is adorned with tinkling bells, bracelets, necklaces, and anklets. //134//
Of the scripture.
(BRK 5.1749) Now, in childhood, youth [is present];
in that which is sweet as the lower lip, the throat [is present] in the throat; with endearments, the eyes [are present] in the eyes.
Having falsely claimed that he was not his son, Kṛṣṇa was placed for a long time upon the chest of the cowherd women, who were filled with agitation as they cried out, "It is but a child!
May He protect us—He whose body is languid with love, smiling and with suppressed horripilation. 135.
O mother of Divākara,
we speak of your conduct: though you assumed the form of a young girl through a disguise, such as you were, bringing joy to the eyes of the fawn-eyed women in the mountain caves.
May Hari, who lies supine before the cowherd girls with his fingers placed upon his own face under the pretext of licking them as they speak thus, purify the world. 136.
Wearing a forest garland;
while the wearer of the forest garland performed deeds befitting childhood upon his father’s lap—
The continuous series of smiles of the ever-new cowherd girls shines forth. //137//
By Śrī Mukunda Bhaṭṭācārya.
(BRK 5.1752) Kṛṣṇa was asked by Yaśodā, "How much fresh butter has been consumed?"
"Only this much," he said, while holding his heavy breasts close to the presence of his elders. //138//
[To someone: "Where are you going, you thief? Surely it is clearly seen that something has been stolen!
You are carrying my second ball here in your bodice."
"Leave it!"—thus exclaiming as he forcibly churns the pair of breasts of the young cowherd girl, Keśava, his body covered in a shimmering mass of horripilation, is victorious in Gokula! //139//
Of Dīpaka. (Spd 74, Smv;
BRK 5.1754) Now, regarding the theft of cow's milk products: [the thief] sees from afar the vessel containing fresh butter.
I worship that indescribable childhood of Keśava, who was filled with agitation as he crawled on his knees, and whose face was turned away out of fear of his mother. 140.
Of a certain [person]:
while stealing butter, seeing the reflection of his own face appearing on a nearby jeweled pillar, he became suspicious out of foolishness, imagining it to be another prince.
"You are indeed my friend; therefore, I have assigned an equal share for you here.
Do not betray me! Do not betray me!"—may the child Hari, thus entreatingly beseeching [the thief], protect you all. 141.
Of some.
Awakened at dawn by the sounds of churning curd,
he entered the cowherds' dwellings with silent steps,
quickly extinguishing the lamps with the breath from his lotus-like mouth.
May Bālakṛṣṇa, who has swallowed fresh butter, protect me. // 142 //
Of someone.
Holding a girdle of tinkling bells with his right hand, bending his body and moving slowly on tiptoe, he laughed softly;
facing those women who were smiling with their faces turned toward him, he checked them with a sidelong glance of his eyes.
Once, Hari took away the fresh butter from behind his mother.
Of the illustrious Śrīmata.
Having taken three or four steps upon the ground at the edge of the doorway,
casting his pair of restless eyes in all directions,
he bears a manifest smile, his mind agitated by the playful act of stealing the curd.
Filled with apprehension, Madhuripu enters the house of the cowherd women.
Of the collector-general.
Rubbing his smooth and fragrant lips— which had stolen the milk and other delicacies— with the touch of his hands,
and repeatedly sniffing them while instantly making his hand rough by rubbing it against his girdle of tinkling bells,
he cast his large eyes with trembling pupils again and again in every direction.
The boy Kūṭagopāla wanders very slowly around his mother's side. // 145 //
Of someone.
Then [the Lord spoke]: "O Hari, you have come as if in a dream;
O Śambhu, welcome, sit here; O Padmodbhava, this way; O Krauñcāri, is all well? O Surapati, are you at ease? O Vitteśa, we do not see you."
May that "thū-thū" sound protect you—the sound made by the mother of the enemy of Kaiṭabha upon hearing these words from her son in a dream:
"My child, what improper things are you prattling? (146)
Of Mayūra:
"O patient Earth, know that the burden of existence has become peaceful;
for indeed, here I am about to strike down the wretched Kaṃsa."
Thus, the wonderful and stilling dreams heard by the cowherd women concerning the infant of Vasudeva are victorious! 147.
Of Sudeva.

(SKM 1.53.2) Now, [the matters of] instructing my parents in wonder and so forth—were they not performed by me on the banks of the Yamunā? Were they not performed by me at the edge of the forest of Śīla? No, indeed; they were.

"Was Kṛṣṇa seen by me at the foot of the banyan tree? "No, he was not seen by me in the courtyard of Rādhā’s father. When the cowherds spoke thus with solemnity, may Hari protect you as he laughed before the astonished Yaśodā’s husband and departed for his own home. 148.
Of Umāpatidhara:
"O child, while wandering in the mountain caves where cattle roam at great distances, you shall behold the ancient Person, Nārāyaṇa, before you, and meditate upon him, seeing the predators ahead."
When he had been addressed thus by Yaśodā, the Enemy of Mura let forth a smile of indistinct meaning from his mouth, due to the force of the firm pressing of his two throbbing bimba-like lips. 149.
Of Abhinanda:
"There was one named Rāma— 'Hum!'— and there was a woman named Sītā— 'Hum!'— while he was dwelling in the Pañcavaṭī forest at his father's command, Rāvaṇa carried her away."
May the agitated words of Saumitri—"The bow! The bow! The bow!"—uttered as he heard his mother recounting this ancient tale of Kṛṣṇa, protect you all. 150.
To someone [he says]:
"O Mother, Śyāmoccandrā sleeps and the child does not come to me; sleep does not come. Listen to a story for the sake of inducing sleep; tell some unprecedented tale."
"Manifesting from the pillar as Narasiṃha, he shall tear asunder the Dānava"—at these words, a smile arises on the face of the Son of Devakī. 151.
Of Sarvānanda.
(SRK 123; SKM 1.52.2; śatānandasya;
BRK 5.1761) Now follows the play of Gorakṣa and others.
The gods, their arms placed upon the heads of single-legged staffs encircled by bracelets,
singing songs of bullfights while wearing crowns upon their heads, followed you with reins,
forming a long continuous line for the combat between two bulls bristling with pride.
May Murāri, in the form of a playful cowherd who has assumed the sport of tending cattle, protect us. //152//
Of the Lord of Yoga:
(SKM 1.5.3) As long as the cowherds, intoxicated by the sweet sound of the flute, drink in Mukunda with all their eyes, whose glances are slow and languid— ah!— so long does he remain.
Meanwhile, the cows, greedy for mouthfuls of tender grass, have gone far away into the interior of the caves and hollows of Mount Govardhana. (153)

The illustrious Keśava was their parasol-bearer. Now follows the excellence of the gopīs’ love: even when He took their names, there was a clinging of their garments to their hips due to their steadfastness.

The discernment of the gopīs; the secret search for a path at the commencement of amorous dalliance; the virtuous conduct of a faithful wife; the searching of the husband's house upon the cessation of play;
such-and-such protection from the Raurava hell; and the longing for the sound of the flute of the enemy of Mura. //154//
Having beheld Kṛṣṇa, the delight of all branches of knowledge, the beautiful-eyed women of Vraja realized that the eyes alone among all the senses possess the true nature of vision.
Having heard that melody of his flute, they desired nothing more than to continue listening. 155.
Of someone [else].
Then, together with the cowherd girls, there was a play in which young women, eager for water-sports in the Yamunā, wore fine Chinese silks.
Having emerged and shaken the water from her limbs, she surveyed all directions;
then, as Śauri watched her for a long time hidden within a bower at the edge of the bank, this significant sound of his flute, causing her agitation, reigns supreme. 156.
Of Puruṣottama-deva;
in them [the verses] is the state of Kṛṣṇa,
arising from the onset of trembling that has begun from his lotus-bud-like hands drenched with perspiration.

May the sound of the flute— emerging from the void of the Enemy of Kaṃsa, whose body is bent in three places as he stands upon his lotus-feet in Vṛndāvana, his heart devoured by the playful, swaying cowherd girls who do not notice that his flute has slipped away— be ever victorious. 157.
The question of Rādhā upon the first sight of the long-lived Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
"O You whose beautiful face is sweet with the art of the dancing of the vine of Your eyebrows!"
With an ear-ornament entwined with a *kaṅkelli* bud, who is this person whose appearance is like a fresh touchstone that, by the sound of his flute, O friend, brings me under his power? (158)
Of someone:
wearing a garment possessing a richness as deep as the interior of a blue lotus, resembling a mass of molten gold.
With a chest adorned by a charming necklace of pearls, who is this youth who makes the world full of the god of love? //159//
Among all those who delight in the arts,
there is no one superior to Sakhī;
yet there is someone else, a suckling infant of the darkness.
He sings with slightly modulated phrases; upon hearing even a little of it, what woman would not have her heart shaken? (160)
A certain person’s preliminary passion for Śrī Rādhā [arises] from the affliction caused by the arrows of the god of love within the mind.
Then Rādhā, her face downcast and manifesting her inner state through the physical transformations of her body, spoke these words in the presence of her circle of friends.
Of the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama:
from the moment that someone of cloud-like luster was beheld in a bower by the Yamunā;
From that time forth, it remains as tremulous as a lotus petal upon the water. //162//
Of Kavicandra.
Accidentally, O friend, as I was walking along a certain path toward the bank of the Yamunā,
I beheld one whose body was dark like a fresh rain-cloud;
I do not know what he did with a sidelong glance, but from that moment this has come to pass.
My mind is restless; it does not settle upon any domestic duty. //163//
Of Jayanta:
first the blue moonlight, followed by the fragrance of musk. (Bhakti-rasāyana; BRS 3.5.27)
Then followed the melodious sound of his playful flute, then the sweet tinkling of his girdle;
thereafter, from the surging waves of the wonder of his body encircled by a creeper of lightning, there arose his loveliness, and after that, his innate bliss. 164.
Of someone:
"O beautiful one, today on the ground of a grove on the bank of the Yamunā, he is intent on amorous play."
Repeatedly playing his flute, Mādhava steals away my heart. //165//
Of someone: From the moment the playful movements of the feet of the enemy of Mura were beheld by his eyes within the grove of cane-bushes on the bank of the Yamunā; (similar to *Premāmṛta* 4.13).
From that time on, my mind does not settle upon any task whatsoever for even a moment; I do not know what ought to be done. //166//
Of Kavicandra:
From the moment the moon-like face of the delighter of the Yadus came within the range of my companion’s eyes, [my heart was captivated].
Until that time, my mind remains naturally averse to reflection, whether toward the Malaya breeze or the fire. //167//
O Sañjaya, crest-jewel of poets!
This has happened— utterly improper, utterly improper, utterly improper!
Thinking him to be a cowherd boy, Hari was gazed upon with curiosity—Hari, Hari! Hari! (168)
Of Śaraṇa.
The face withers, the pair of thighs grows numb,
the heart trembles, and the surface of the cheeks perspires, O friend.
Wearing a forest garland, what did he behold? //169//
By Mukunda Bhaṭṭācārya:
O friend, above the tamāla tree,
there is a certain orb of the full autumnal moon.
And therein, the practice of playing the flute brings the family's moral boundaries to ruin. //170//
O Sañjaya, crest-jewel of poets!
Alas, my mind desires to see even that beloved one, yet it is not right on account of him.
O moon-faced one, both the gentle breeze and the sandalwood paste spread only agony. //171//
For someone, there was the disparagement of elders, infamy, and some terrible conduct befitting a householder.
O Śiva, Śiva! The flute of the enemy of Mura causes all that to be forgotten. // 172 //
Of all those who delight in the sciences:
wealth, residence, offspring, as well as friends and noble birth.
The wearer of the forest garland does not cause the eyes of Upayamunā to dance as long as [he does not act]. //173//
May my enemies find their satisfaction in those very [faults] by discovering my flaws; may the lord of the house take up the burden of governing my home.
