The lotus-eyed one reached Vraja. //258//
Of someone.

In that very place was the good fortune of Rādhā; for on the road, she was honored by one with the movement of her creeper-like eyebrows, by another with the opening of her eyes, and by another with the moonlight of her smile.

Victorious are the glances of the Enemy of Kaṃsa, which fall with trembling supplication upon the face of Rādhā—a face that possesses the splendor of modesty yet treats him with disdain due to his arrogance in creating a rift. //259//
By Umāpatidhara:

With his neck bent sideways, his ear-ornaments touching the region of his shoulders, his mass of hair uplifted by shimmering peacock feathers, and possessing the playful grace of curved creeper-like eyebrows;
May the face of Viṣṇu in the form of a cowherd protect you—his lips set to a humming flute, and his closed eyes fixed with intent upon the face of Rādhā. //260//

Of King Lakṣmaṇasena. (SKM 1.55.2) With her cheeks resting upon the flute held against her shoulder, a sweet sound was produced by the gentle breeze set in motion by the pair of her bimba-red lips pressed against her mouth.

May the husband of Rādhā protect you—he whose multitude of necklaces sway with a slight curvature, and whose mass of fingers bends, moves, and rises toward each and every opening of her lotus-like mouth. //261//
Of Nāthoka.
With her fingers restrained by the tip of her thumb, she pressed down upon the ground with the sole of her foot,
thoroughly moistening the edge of her garment with the immediate drops of milk.
O friend, Dāmodara milks the cow, the sound of the stream falling into the hollow of his mouth—held between his two knees pressed together—is enchanting. 262.
Of Śaraṇa: (SKM 5.1.1;
Srk 1157, by Upādhyāya Dāmarasvāmin;
UN 10.50) Upon hearing the tinkling of whose jeweled girdle, the deceitful ones suddenly [fled].
That you became so slack in the grip of your arms even while embracing—
how can I describe this? My friend, reeling from the poison of your many words composed of ghee and honey, is no longer capable of attending to anything at all.
Of someone... (Amaru 73/109,
SD 3.37) [Description of] the deceitful hero (*śaṭha-nāyaka*), and then the lifting of Govardhana.
He was gazed upon by Yaśodā with eyes full of joy at his beloved qualities; by Rādhā, who watched him with affection;
by the cowherd boys, who eagerly honored him with displays of their own prowess;
and by Nanda, who looked on with a mixture of fear, joy, and wonder.
May Hari protect you—he who, with playful grace, rests upon the great mountain situated upon his lotus-like hand. //264//
Of Sonnokasya (or Sollokasya, or Sonnokasya).
"O Kṛṣṇa, this Govardhana has been held up by you alone for a long time;
you are weary, so rest now for a moment while all of us here blow [the flutes].
When the multitude of cowherds had thus raised their arms, with Kṛṣṇa slightly contracting his own arm—
May Hari, smiling as he cries out while oppressed by the weight of the mountain slanting downward, protect you all. //265//
Of Śaraṇa:
"You are exhausted; let go of the mountain!
We shall carry it," they said, and his arms grew slack.
Victorious is Hari, smiling as the cowherds stretch out their arms, bent down by the weight [of the mountain]. // 266 //
O Govardhana, you who bear [the mountain], vanish far from the path of Hari's vision! (Subandhu; also attributed to Haribhāskara and Śrīharṣa)
"O slender-waisted one, let this [garland] not slip from his hand while his gaze is fixed upon you"—

may those breaths of the Enemy of Kaṃsa protect you, breaths which, as he perceived the murmurs of the gopīs regarding the concealment of Rādhā, caused him to falter under the exhaustion of supporting the mountain. 267.
Of Śubhaṅka.
Now, the boat-game:
"Go to the further shore of the Yamunā."
Victorious is Hari, who, called by the cowherd women with cries of "Wait a moment!", feigns sleep on the riverbank and redoubles his laziness. 268.
Of Sañjayakaviśekhara:
(BRK 5.1706) "Arise quickly, young woman; what power do I have to climb my tree? O innocent one, I tell you plainly: here, under the name of the sun, what pleasure is there for me in the sun?"

"Perhaps some news regarding us might somehow arise; even a mere report concerning our meeting would suffice"—with these words, I propitiate Rādhā, whose smiling face has conquered Mount Kailāsa and who remains unconquered herself. 269.
That you said, "The daughter of the sun is a new boat released by a multitude of waves," is indeed the truth;
yet this very thing is the cause of my excessive apprehension.
And you, O Mādhava, are fickle because you are a sailor here. //270//
These two belong to the Collector:
an old boat on a river with exceedingly deep waters, and we who are young; thus, all this is a cause of misfortune.
O Mādhava, this alone is the seed of deliverance for those with slender waists: that you yourself are now their helmsman. //271//
Of Jagadānanda Rāya:
that son of Devakī, who stayed the sun upon the waters of the Yamunā; (BRK 5.1709)
Smiling, he gazes at the face of the cowherd girl who is distressed by her separation from her husband.
O delight of the Yadus,
by my own word, both the load of cattle and the necklace were suddenly scattered by me in the water for you alone.
And although the silken garment has been drawn far away from these two breasts,
it is nevertheless not far from the bank of the daughter of Kalinda.
For someone [who says]:
"This boat, its rolling suddenly stilled by the winds, enters the deep waters of the Yamunā, which are filled to the brim with floods of milk."
"Alas, what a cruel fate for me! Even though my heart is overcome by supreme curiosity, Hari claps his hands again and again. (274)
O Manoharā,
even though my hands do not rest at all during the act of sprinkling water, your words are still full of jest.
If I should live again, O Kṛṣṇa, then never at any time shall I place my feet upon your sun-like radiance. //275//
With reference to Him alone: "Friends, bow down to your own chosen deity for this purpose. (Premāmṛta 3.12; BRK 5.1712)
Let the Yamunā itself be knee-deep, or let there be no other ferryman at all. //276//
Of Mukunda Bhaṭṭācārya:
The boat is the river Uttaralā, deep and vast;
the helmsman is the son of Nanda, who is as steady as a gem.
The sun, O friend, is setting upon me, a weak woman; the city is still far away—what shall I do here? //277//
Of someone.

He pays no heed to words of praise, he does not listen to plaintive entreaties, and he constantly disregards every prostration made before him; alas, my friend, what can be done now? The son of Nanda!
In the midst of the river, the fickle one shakes his boat. //278//
Of that very [person].
An extra verse found in only one edition:
"For the sake of crossing over and for the sake of lightness."
O Destroyer of Mura, I take refuge in you; why do you pay homage to another? There is no trust to be placed in a mere boatman.
"O someone!
Here is the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā), her banks' slopes leaped over by lofty waves;
this boat is filled with water, for there is no fear even of a stain from Hari."
"O beautiful one, do not be hard-hearted today; O Rādhā, we clearly live by your grace. Please grant us the festival of pleasure in the mountain valleys. (279)
Why do you make this whimpering sound, O rogue, with your limbs hidden in a heap of dried cow-dung in the corner of the house? Go away in vain!
Where today [is there safety] for one terrified by the wandering of the aged sun?
The skill in mimicking the assembly of cowherd women. //280//
Three [verses] of Samāhartṛ.
Now follows the dialogue between Hari and Rādhā:
"Who strikes the door-panel with his finger, O crooked one? "Mādhava. "Is it springtime?"

"Are you not a wheel-bearer? Is the potter not so? Are you not the upholder of the earth? Is the lord of serpents not double-tongued? Am I not the crusher of terrible snakes? Are you not the lord of birds? Am I not Hari? Is the lord of monkeys not so?"—may the wielder of the discus, his face thus smiling at the words of Rādhā, protect you all. 281.
To someone [he said]:
"Who are you, O Keśava, appearing in the night? Why do you pride yourself on your hair?"
"O auspicious lady, I am Śauri by virtue of my father's qualities; what does that matter here for a son?
O moon-faced one, you give me a wheel-maker’s [vessel], but not a water-pot, a jar, or a milking vessel.
May Hari, who was thus abashed by the cowherd girl's superior retort, protect you all. 282.
O Keśava, where now is the garment of Cakrapāṇi? "O lovely-eyed one, this indeed is the garment; tell me, O rogue, for it has become exceedingly beautiful through contact with your limbs."
"Where did you spend the night, O rogue? What does the bodiless one steal from the night?
"The Lord of the Śauris (Viṣṇu), while joking with such deceits as these, protects you—the cowherd's wife. //283//
To someone [He says]:
"O Rādhā, you are angry; indeed, you alone are angry. You are the mother of the earth, for you alone are the mother of the worlds; there is no other who knows [this]."

"O Goddess, in this playful quarrel of our amorous sport, you alone are infinite"; smiling thus, Śauri bowed to the beautiful cowherd girl—who is none other than Śrī herself—may he bring about your prosperity. //284//
Of Hari-Hara.
(From SKM 1.56.1 by Vākpati;
Srk 108) Now, the *rāsa* dance: in the forest of Vṛndāvana, the abode of the joyful, amidst the fragrance of *mallikā* flowers.

At night, amidst the beautiful light of the rays of the illustrious moon and the charming songs of cuckoos and other birds, the king of sweet flute-playing belonging to the enemy of Kaṃsa shone forth, stealing away the hearts and bodies of the women of Vraja. 285.
To someone,
this sound of Hari’s flute in his pastimes is the preeminent bearer of the sweetness of the nectar of the lower lip.
It spread a great joy of mind among the female deer,
the fawn-eyed women, and the sages.
Of the venerable Śrī Mādhavendrapurīpāda:
the multitude of cowherd women whose hearts were captivated by the flute made resonant through his divine play.
May Kṛṣṇa, who thirsts for the honey upon her lower lip, protect you from the abyss of worldly existence. // 287 //
Of Mādhava-cakravartin.
O Mother, do not delay;
grant me permission to depart for Hari.
I cannot endure remaining here, since he is there.
The flute resounds like a bold female messenger. //288//
Of the collector-general.
His beautiful hair kisses his crest-jewel; he wears a garment with the luster of gold;
a *karṇikāra* flower adorns his ear; he is agitated by the god of love;
his face is eloquent in the playing of the flute; and his glances are cast askance.
Those of fickle middles took refuge in the interior of the groves as their fortune reached its end. // 289 //
The words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the army of the servants of the living beings:
"I suspect that some wicked person repeatedly causes you humiliation in Gokula."

"O you who have come running into the forest at night with your garments slipping—ah, what fear is there? On my arm, which bears the imprint of the vermilion from the wives of the great Dānavas, shines the mark of the deer-eyed woman as she sports in her husband's embrace. (290)

While the dense, pure stream of Dharma flows with the heat of ascetic purification, what thirst remains within the heart? O women of noble character, do not yield to such intoxication; long for the homes of virtuous wives and do not act in opposition to them.
Alas, this path of merit does not conflict with my view! (291)
Now follows the reply of the Vraja goddesses:
"Why do you instruct us in the path that leads to righteousness? Be gracious and teach your own disciple, Muralī, whose face is exceedingly gentle."
Alas, alas! This bold woman, who transgresses all bounds and draws our hearts toward the Supreme Person, does not call out to us, O best of the Yadus. (292)
Three belong to the collector-general.
With his waist embraced by the gopīs, blowing his flute with eyes intensely rolling,
and with the hair on his body standing erect—
I bow to Kṛṣṇa, the sole root of the world. //293//
Of the illustrious Lord Puruṣottama.
Of the enemy of Kaṃsa, who followed Rādhikā as she left the Rasa dance on the banks of the Kālindī, angry during their play and departing with tears clouding her eyes;
he whose feet were placed upon the impressions of her footprints, and from whom a thrill of hair stood erect.
May that unbroken affection of the beloved wife, who gazes upon him with a serene look, nourish you all. // 294 //
Of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa.
(Veṇīsaṃhāra 1.2) Upon Kṛṣṇa’s disappearance, their question:
"O Tulasī, you shine; O Mallikā, you have blossomed."
O land-lotus-pond, you shine with your body joined to the bee;
tell us quickly, O friends, in which cave does that son of Nanda, that rogue-lotus-root, dwell among us? (295)
"O friend, it has been seen that Mādhava has gone somewhere, taking one of the women of Vraja with him; indeed, we have all been deceived. If he is to be sought out... (UN 10.94)
Having cried out, "Go, both of you," Hari suddenly took Rādhā by the hand and, assuming the guise of a cowherd girl, entered the depths of the forest bower; may He protect you. 296.
The words of Rādhā’s friend to someone:
"If you abandon her in the forest, whether out of fault or without fault..."
O Lord of the three worlds, who can tell you whether it was auspicious or inauspicious?
But this cruel heart of mine remembers that for your sake, O ornament of your lineage, she did not even consider her own self in the wilderness. (297)
By Rāmacandradāsa:
Expanding his own splendor within the circle of the rāsa dance by means of his central position,
he is fragrant with musk, his moon-like face resting upon the playful flute.
May Hari, who sports with eyes delighted by the circle of his playful *tāṇḍava* dance seen all around, protect you with his feet crowded with the rhythmic movements of the *hallīśaka*. 298.
Of someone.
Therein is the speech of the sky-goers;
it is to be sought by liberated sages.
Devakī bears a certain fruit;
Yaśodā protects it, and the gopīs enjoy it to their heart's content. //299//
Of one from the South.
The fruit of the penances performed by others has ripened upon the jar-like breasts of these cowherd girls.
Brahman envelops [all] in blue. //300//
Of the venerable Upādhyāya Raghupati.
Now follows the water-sport:
his face repeatedly covered and then uncovered by Rādhikā’s hand, which was restless in the play of the water.
May Kṛṣṇa, who delights in the separation and reunion of the pair of cakravāka birds, protect the world. //301//
(UN 15.235) An envious remark by a friend of Candrāvalī to a friend of Rādhā:
"Do not harbor such pride; it shines upon the surface of your cheek."
"This is 'The Fresh Cluster' written by Kṛṣṇa’s own hand.
"Friend, would not even another woman be a fit vessel for such things, were it not for the obstacle of trembling within? (302)
Of Dāmodara.
(Amaru 55; SKM 2.140.5 by Keśaṭa;
SD 3.105 *mada*; Daśa 2.22, etc.; BRS 2.4.165):
The words of Rādhā’s friend, full of intentional meaning: "From the time when [He] was all around Gokula..."
From that time on, this Candrāvalī became one who was beloved for her yellow garment, like a row of flower-strewn seats. //303//
Of Govardhanācārya. (Aryā verses 436/531) A friend’s words to Candrāvalī: "We have been won over by your goodness; therefore, we shall say something to you."
O beautiful one, if you go to the Kālindī, do not go again to the grove of Kadamba trees;
for there is a certain mass of utterly pure darkness therein, and when it slightly touches the edge of the eyes of the lotus-eyed woman, she cannot see her husband’s home.
Of Govinda-bhaṭṭa.
"This day is dark with masses of clouds; it is evening. "Nevertheless, O friend, you go to the bank of the Yamunā for the sake of flowers, full of longing. "Go! What pain is there for me?
"But rather, upon seeing even a single wound on my breast from a sharp thorn, [she would immediately think] otherwise."
Since a crooked person will harbor suspicion, I have become distressed because of him.
Of Karṇapūra.
If the Yamunā is in your mind, you must go there; then, O naturally simple one, do not go to the *vāñjula* grove at my word.
Or, alas, if you would rather go even there, O noble one, go to Murāri!
Somewhere in solitude, you might hear the sound of a flute. //306//
Do not delay for one whose poetry has not been enjoyed;
remembering the jar, go to your home.
So long as the flute of the enemy of Kaṃsa does not utter its enchanting mantra.
Of the collector-general.
Leaning on a *nīpa* tree with his back toward the Yamunā, Mukunda plays the flute of delight upon her banks,
while she tosses a water-pot in the water before it is filled.
It turns away the face of the cowherd woman.
Of someone.
O son of Nanda, when I was carrying a very large, full water-pot to my friends' house, I became exhausted; if you touch me while I am alone, [what will happen]?
I shall suddenly release this life-force before you. //309//
Of the collector-general.
This is the speech of someone directed toward her:
"The sandalwood paste on your breasts has been swept away by your swaying forest garland,
and the crocodile-pattern painted on your cheeks has been destroyed by the swinging of the crocodile-shaped earring."
"O rogue, this slender body of yours is exhausted by its playful, languid waves; you speak the truth, for today you have become immersed in joy while gazing at the daughter of the Sun. (310)
Of the collector-general.
This is the speech of a female friend addressed to her husband:
"O fortunate one, why do you look again and again with apprehension at my dear friend?"
Her back is tawny with the pollen from the beloved’s fingernails, scattered by the breeze from the Yamunā. //311//
Of the collector-general.
To Candrāvalī, she said:
"Out of a desire for the flowers of Kātyāyanī, why have you gone out of curiosity into the hollow depths of the forest?"
Look, O fair-throated one! Alas, the cowherd, having become angry, sees the marks of thorns upon your two bud-like breasts. (312)
These belong to the Collector; now,
the eternal pastimes of Mukunda shine forth in Vṛndāvana as his eternal play.
This is clearly not spoken even by those who know it, because of its secret nature.
"By means of those lotus-faced women of the cowherd settlement, Mādhava perpetually extends his dwelling in Vṛndāvana"— thus Hara spoke somewhat jokingly to his beloved.
Behold, how great is the secret of the jewel of the pastimes of the Lord of Vraja!
Even though he was a knower of reality, the son of Vyāsa explained his departure to another city.
For thus did Hara speak in secret to Pārvatī in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "There, where the slayer of Kaṃsa sports in the company of cows, cowherds, and gopīs."

Now, regarding the departure of Hari for Mathurā, these are the words of Rādhā’s friend: "This very day, you have caused the body of this poor girl to attain a likeness to the crescent moon risen on the first day of the lunar fortnight."
O flower-arrowed one, now that Kṛṣṇa has departed, tell me: where will you discharge your volley of arrows at dawn? //313//
Of Rudra:
Departure has been made by her bracelets; she has gone with her dear friends;
not for a moment has she sat still through fortitude; her mind has resolved to go on ahead.
When the beloved has resolved in her mind to go, everyone sets out together;
for when one must depart, why should the caravan of life, dear ones, and friends be abandoned? 314.
Of the Immortal One. (Amaru 31/36;
Sbhv 1151;
She whose very shadow did not come within the range of his vision when Hari entered Mathurā—
that same bride now adorns the center of the city.
Moreover, having perceived Mukunda in the city of Mathurā, even a blind man proceeds there with the hand of a kinsman placed upon his own hand. //315//
Of Vāṇīvilāsa.
Therein is the speech of a city woman:
"To shed tears incessantly..."
Fie upon our ears and eyes!
That youthfulness of his, which ought to have been seen, has already been fully beheld by the women of Vraja. (316)
For one who has not eaten by them.

Blessed are those young women of Vraja who, out of curiosity, behold that Brahman which is intense bliss, infinite, imperishable, and unborn— the supreme reality which even yogis, single-minded in meditation, strive to perceive directly for a moment every day.
They embrace, converse, pull [him] by the hair a hundred times, and kiss him. //317//
Of the lord of the army.
[Extra verse:
The sole root of bliss, the essence of all the Vedas.

Alas, the cowherd women, who are heaps of merit, having drawn forth the inner lamp— which is exceedingly difficult to cross and resembles collyrium— from within their dense breasts, have embraced it and attained their desire.
Dear friend, it is clear that the son of Nanda, being of perverse character, did not go with this city-dweller;
he is like a pond whose lotus petals have not yet been crushed.
Just as when the forest edge is still possessed of unblemished new shoots. //318//
Of the prince.
I heard his confident words, "I shall go," as he prepared to depart;
as he walked far away, I watched him again and again, even turning back to look. Yet when he had vanished from sight, I returned to this empty house, and only my life-breaths remain.
"Friends, look! Out of hypocrisy, I weep for my beloved life. (319)
From Rudraṭa:
"One watch has passed; two watches have passed; many watches have passed; the day has gone."
Alas, woe! What shall I do?
I do not behold the face of Hari.
Of Śaṅkara.
O friend, tossing a flower-ball like a dancer on the banks of the Yamunā, he will not be seen again.
The moon-like youth of the deceitful cowherd. //321//
The sixth [case ending] is used for the servant.
"O friend, those women who see their beloved in a dream are truly blessed; but for us, now that Kṛṣṇa has departed— "
Even sleep, that enemy, has departed.
For the fortunate one: this is that very season of spring; this is that same forest;
this is that same tree in the bower; and all of that remains as it was.
Alas! But why is this first incarnation of the Flower-Arrowed God, with limbs as tender as a fresh rain-cloud, not being beheld? //323//
Of Sañjaya, the crest-jewel of poets.
A single blink of the eye has become like an eon;
the entire world has become like a desolate wilderness.
Because of my separation from Govinda. //324//
Of the Blessed One: (Śikṣāṣṭaka, 7) My heart breaks with intense agitation, yet it does not split in two;
my body, though failing, carries on, and though fainting, it does not lose consciousness.
The internal burning consumes the body but does not reduce it to ashes; fate strikes with a blow that severs the vital organs but does not cut short one's life. //325//
Cause the clouds to swirl, filled with their inner waters; gladden the cātaka birds.

O pitiless one, sharpen the cries of the peacocks and harden the ketaka flowers; having caused a fainting fit in those separated from their lovers, why do you seek to dispel their pain by inflicting the disease of consciousness once again? 326.
These two [verses] are by Bhavabhūti (*Mālatīmādhava* 9.42; *Spd* 3453;
*Smv* 43.34): "The sky has been seen, grey with the pollen of *ketaka* flowers; gradually, [the clouds] have been beheld..."
I have endured the *kaccānta* winds carrying the scent of *śilīndhra* and *kandalī* flowers, and the breezes from the *kadamba* trees;
O friends, restrain your tears and cast away your fear—why this agitation? For now, I am surely as firm as adamant, and I shall endure even these [seasons] with fortitude. (327)
Of Rudra:
This is that river; those very same bees are the bees of the night-lotuses;
this is that bank of the Yamunā; this is that forest.
Those breezes, fragrant with jasmine—alas, O beloved of my life, you alone have become so difficult to attain! //328//
Of Haribhaṭṭa.
O Lord of the Yadus,
when will my dwellings, having rushed forth from all sides simultaneously, proclaim that you have arrived?
With the orbs of their moon-like faces blooming. //329//
By them, [the merit] of one who has not eaten is [attained].
O Lord, compassionate toward the wretched, O Lord of Mathurā, when will you be seen? My heart is distressed by the longing for your sight.
My beloved wanders about; what can I do? //330//
O companion, this separation from the Moon of the Cowherds does not spread such intense agony within me as does the memory of the feet of Śrī Mādhavendrapurī. (CC 2.4.197, 3.8.32)
Just as his dwelling was in the city of the Lord of the Danujas, which is surrounded by circles of bitter asuras. //331//
By Śrī Raghunātha Dāsa:
Alas, as this ever-new mango sprout quivers,
even the life-force itself will become exceedingly fickle in nature.
But there was one single, no small sorrow for me: that he has not departed together with the lord of my life. (332)
Hanging by a single thread of hope,
I preserve my life only if there were a fixed limit.
If Brahmā is the sole benefactor of all the world, for what purpose did he create this Kālakūṭa poison? //333//
O breeze, waft the cool and fragrant scent of the kunda flowers from Hari;
O moon, reveal the quarters of the sky; O god of love, manifest yourself at will!
"The day of our tryst has come; friends, abandon talk of him, for now my heart desires to do something else here. (334)
O friend, if the Lord of the Yadus does not come, let him not come; if my life-breaths depart due to separation from him, let them depart— at the will of Rudra.
This alone is a supreme and great thunderbolt-strike upon my heart: that I have not yet beheld her moon-like face once more.
Of Hari-bhaṭṭa.
Let this body attain the state of the five elements, and let the hosts of beings clearly dissolve into their own respective portions;
having prostrated with my head before the Creator, I beg of him even this further boon:
that there may be water in his ponds, light in his mirror, and [fragrance] in his courtyards.
In the sky was the void, on its path was the earth, and at its handle was the wind. // 336 //
Or, having embraced me— who am devoted to your feet— may he crush me for six months.
Let him strike my vital organs out of sight,
or let that lecher do as he pleases;
nevertheless, he alone is the lord of my life, and no other.
From the Śrī Bhagavat-purāṇa (CC 3.20.47, UN 13.79): A statement of Kṛṣṇa upon remembering Yaśodā in Mathurā:
"Who would place half-chewed betel from their own mouth into my mouth?"
Who could bring me, who have strayed onto the wrong path, under their control with flattering words?
Who, stretching out their arms from afar and calling "Come, come!", would now take me onto their lap and, shaking off my crest-ornament loosened in play, bind it back for me once more? (338)
Of that which has not been eaten by them.
Then, by the remembrance of Śrī Rādhā, Hari spoke these words:
"If, through the ripening of my merit, I should somehow find a secluded forest or a desolate wilderness that is devoid of travelers for a long time..."
O moon-faced one, with your tears flowing incessantly, mingled with the sound of your sobbing, I shall flood the worlds with your sorrows. //339//
By them, [the merit] of one who has not yet eaten his meal [is consumed].
Hari’s words to Uddhava:
"Among those attached to sense objects, there are first the women;
among them, the cowherd girls (gopīs), whose speech is naturally gentle."
She was in their midst,
and within her, too, there was something gazed upon by him.
Of someone.
Uddhava’s message from Hari to Rādhā:
On the day of His manifestation, He did not take even the slightest cause into account;
nor does His policy diminish through the commission of offenses, nor does His wisdom increase through prostration.
How indeed can I now avoid the meanness of mere words toward that Guru, who has revealed the nectar [of truth] and who destroys the suffering of the three worlds? (341)
Of some.
Let alone being a fit vessel for the composition of words; let even the possibility of an embrace of your body remain far, far away.
Yet, with repeated prostrations, I beg this of you: that you be made compliant.
Remembering again and again, even for me there is some trace in the calculation of my own kinsmen. //342//
Of Keśava Bhaṭṭācārya.
The words of Uddhava as he was departing for Vṛndāvana:
"This is that Yamunā, sweet and glossy as the petals of a blue lotus,
affectionate toward the water-rainbows [cranes] trembling with cries of joy and blinded by passion."
In ancient times, on whose bank the days of Murabhid were mostly spent with impetuous longing through the pleasure of sporting with the cowherd girls. //343//
In the city of Daśaratha (or Śaraṇa),
this Yamunā, its waters rendered turbid day after day by the bodily pigments from the breasts of the young wives of Vraja, became one of shifting currents.
Oh! Now that this enemy of Mura has departed, the ocean has become doubly dark with the water of collyrium that constantly flowed from the weeping of those women.
Of Sarvānanda.
This is that very sandbank of the Yamunā, where Gokula once became so transfixed by listening to the fame of the slayer of the demon Kaṃsa that they forgot to swallow their mouthfuls;
it was a place made sweet and smooth by the sound of the whirling flute, heard with rapturous ears.
It was being incessantly stirred in every direction by the cowherd girls, who were singing melodiously. //345//
To those beloveds of the cowherd, to whom [the world] pays homage—by whose very qualities, when contemplated, [all things are transformed]. (Moṭaka; SKM 5.11.5 Keśaṭa)
On the chest of the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Vaijayantī garland withers from his hot sighs. (Verse 346) — by someone.
Uddhava’s words to the family of the Vraja goddesses:
"Even yogis are not able to traverse the path of you who are separated from Him."
For you have reached the state of the object of meditation—the supreme Person who is himself the object of meditation—which is difficult to attain. //347//
Of someone.

Upon seeing Uddhava, Rādhā spoke to her friend: "O companion, what auspicious news shall I tell you? For in the past, during our private moments, you constantly invoked the name of the enemy of Mura as the Lord of my life."
Out of fear that my love might be shattered, even upon seeing my beloved, I ask nothing at all, remaining in doubt as to whether I have been sent by the Lord’s messenger or not. 348.
Of Rāmacandra-dāsa.
Uddhava’s words to Śrī Rādhā:
"O lady with thighs like the trunk of an elephant, do not soil your moon-like face with the tears from your eyes."
Hari, the abode of the ocean of compassion, will show you even greater mercy. //349//
"Sixth [case]: of the servant. (UN 12.30) This is the speech of Rādhā’s friend addressed to Uddhava:
"Of her who rests one cheek upon the palm of her hand..."
For that lotus-eyed woman, whose face was bathed by the tears from her unceasing eyes, how could there have been even a moment of sleep for Mādhava from the very day of his auspicious departure? 350.
Of Hari and Hara. (BRS 3.5.32) This message regarding Kṛṣṇa is from Rādhā’s friend alone:
"Even the houses of the merchants are devoid of sandalwood paste."

The forest regions of every quarter have become devoid of sprouts, and the banks of the rivers and lakes have become free of lotuses; yet, due to the agony of separation from him, no peace has arisen. 351.
Of that very [person].

In former times, you were the very life-breath of the worlds, and even for Hari, you became the spiritual preceptor who showed the path to the fair-browed women of Vraja by taking up the sound of his flute;
O friend, breeze from the pleasure-gardens of Mathurā, even now you belong to the Lord of Śrī.
With your limbs purified by touch and your body cool, you alone are our protector. //352//
Of Rāmacandra-dāsa.
The message is from Rādhā’s friend herself to Kṛṣṇa:
"With my hair standing on end from the gentle breeze that has come from your region,
I am satiating my eyes upon a beautiful picture-board marked with your form."

With her ear-cavities sprinkled by the nectar of your name and her gaze fixed upon the window of your path, that slender woman remains day and night with her voice filled with the singing of the *pañcama* note. //353//
Of Trivikrama.
The fire of the fever of love is in her limbs; the mudrā of meditation is in her eyes; her life-breath is in her throat; her cheek rests long upon her sprout-like hand.
The braid remains on her shoulder, the sandalwood paste upon the region of her breasts, and silence in her speech; yet all of this, as well as her heart, exists nowhere at all without you.
Of Kṣemendra.
When the moon was seen, the darkness vanished; when you, whose pure brilliance flashes forth, stood in the courtyard of the sky as your own beloved, you departed far away.
Her breath acts like a night-lily bud, her face acts like a lotus, her love-god acts like the ocean of milk, and even her glance instantly acts like a moonstone. //355//
Of Bhīmabhaṭṭa.
O Mukunda, how can I describe the fever of this lotus-eyed woman to you, when her heart— already scorched— is pressed against a fresh lotus petal?
First it dries up and subsequently shrinks; then it turns to powder, and afterwards, assuming the state of embers, the fire, fanned by the breath, burns. //356//
Of Śāntikara. (Smv 44.25; SKM 2.31.1; Srk 553 by someone;
[verse attributed to] Utpalarāja)
The slender vine of her body is not fanned with a lotus leaf for fear it might be shaken;
her limbs are not sprinkled with sandalwood paste water for fear they might burst;
and generally, fresh shoots are not placed upon her for fear she might be overwhelmed by their excessive weight.
The wound is upon your breast; how then can this affliction be endured by one of such slender frame? 358.
Of Ānanda.
If that Rādhā dwells within your heart— which is forged of diamond—
then indeed all is well with her.
[They were] being struck by the arrows of Love. //359//
Of someone:
"They are opening [their eyes]—pluck them with your nails! They are moving along—cover them with the hem of your silken garment!
They are entering the pleasure-grove—startle them with the tinkling of your bracelets!"
Thus, O fortunate one, during your separation, the symbolic conversations of Rādhā’s friends with one another take place among the young leaves, the southern breeze, and the cuckoos. (360)
Of Śambhu: (SKM 2.30.4; Amaru; Spd 3489; Smv 44.13;
SD 10.79) "One fainting fit fades away, while another arises again—this being the case for these two..."

O fortunate one, even though the entire night passed, there was some portion of the middle watch remaining while she was drawing this love-letter for you with flower-arrows; yet, not even the first part of the word "Svasti" (well-being) reached completion.
When you were meditated upon by the son of Tanu for Citra’s sake, the Lord of Śacī drew his bow with its string stretched,
and as he approached with the pair of fingers to grasp the bowstring, the arrow was fixed upon the cord.

O Keśava, while your wondrous work was being commenced, she—pierced by the arrows released from your bow—clung tightly to the wall and remained there for a long time as if depicted in a painting. 362.
Of Bāṇa [the King of Siṃhala]: Thinking that you, who have been transformed by internal, steady contemplation, were standing right before him,
he was about to impetuously embrace you with his circle of arms when—
I believe that even the clouds, having soon embraced their own bodies and seeing them covered in horripilation, wept under the guise of rainwater. 363.
For someone:
Tears were shed unrestrained for kinsmen; the heat of sorrow was placed upon her friends; wretchedness was deposited entirely upon her attendants; and anxiety was entrusted to her elders.
"She will surely attain liberation today or tomorrow; she is now distressed by her final breaths.
Be confident, for the sorrow born of separation has been shared by her. (364)
Now, her speech, uttered out of jealous anger at his very touch, is as follows:
In Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, who forcibly captivates the hearts of others through the abundance of sweetness in his countenance.
For one who desires friendship, what hope can there be for the body? //365//
Of Jagannāthasena.
Now follows the message of the Vraja goddesses, delivered with irony:
"What is the use of words that are distressed by the hardship of being heard by a third person?"
Or what is the use of a gaze made bitter by a mere blink?
O Lord, son of Nanda, for the beautiful women of Gokula, it is devotion to you alone that moves within their hearts and accompanies them. 366.
Of someone;
or else, it is a message according to the facts—
she who [is reached] by the sweet sounds of the flute.
O Mādhava, how can those cowherd girls pass the time during their separation from you, disregarding even the weight of their shame toward their teacher? 367.
[This is] the sixth slave.
O traveler to Mathurā, hear again at the gateway these words of the cowherd girls concerning Murāri,
as he stands once more by the waters of the Yamunā.
The fire of Kāliya’s venom blazes forth. // 368 //
Of Vīrasarasvatī. (SKM 1.62,5;
UN 10.98) Now, the separation of Hari while staying in Dvāravatī:
[he beheld] the Kalindī river, whose gentle current flows favorably, and which is dark as a blue lotus.

May Dāmodara, the Lord of Dvārakā— who, feeling remorse as he remembers Rādhā sweet with her first secret tryst and the fragrant slopes of the mountain caves filled with *kadamba* blossoms— be for the delight of the three worlds. (369)
Of Śaraṇa:

He does not desire pleasure at will, he does not rejoice in the lotus-pond of dalliance, he does not take delight in the outpourings of moonlight, nor does he even long for the playful conversation of deer-eyed women.
Sinking during the nights with a body lacking strength, Hari, the infatuated one, languishes with limbs too weary for the desire of enjoyment, his mind fixed upon the cowherd girl.
Of Him alone—
when He was embraced by Rukmiṇī in the palace at Dvārakā, whose ocean-like waters were dappled with the luster of jewels, and who experienced a powerful eruption of horripilation.
May the world be protected by the swoon of Murāri, caused by meditating upon the fullness of the fragrance of Rādhā’s pastimes in the bower of cane thickets on the smooth banks of the Yamunā. 371.
By Umāpatidhara. (SKM 1.61.1;
UN 14.184; Jīva and VCT to BRS 2.4.178) "While submerged in the water, I embraced the bank out of affection—by whom was this falsehood told to you today, O Rādhā? You suffer in vain."
May that embrace of Rukmiṇī’s neck—loosened with feigned anger when she heard the words of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow as she lay among a succession of festival dreams—protect you. 372.
By Umāpatidhara (or by someone else).
SKM version:
Out of fear of Love, I embraced my friend while submerged in the water.
"Who told you this falsehood today, Rādhā? Why do you suffer in vain?
Hearing these words of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow in a succession of dreams while lying on the bed, Kamalā feignedly loosened her embrace of his neck—may that protect you! (By someone).
Now follows the song of separation from the Sovereign of Vṛndāvana: When the Enemy of Mura had departed for the city of Dvāravatī, she, longing and wrapped in His garment,
clung to a vañjula creeper in a grove on the bank of the Kālindī.
Rādhā sang with a loud voice faltering with heavy tears,
such that even the aquatic creatures moving within the water cried out in longing.
Of Aparājita.
(From SKM 1.58.4 by Kasyacit; Dhvanyaloka, Vakroktijīvita 2.59; etc.;
UN 14.188) Now follows the message of the cowherd women:
"O traveler, if you are going to Dvāravatī, then [inform] the son of Devakī."
It must be said that even the cowherd girls, rendered helpless by the mantra of the delusion of love, did not abandon Your name;

yet these regions on the banks of the Yamunā, where the quarters of the sky are obscured by the masses of pollen from the *kadamba* trees used in Your pastimes, do not come within the range of Your mind. 374.
Of Govardhanācārya.

Those caves of Govardhana, that bank of the Yamunā, that Bhāṇḍīra tree which was the essence of his pastimes, that lord of trees, those companions, and that courtyard of the cow-pen— [all these I remember].
"O serpent of Dvāravatī, does his heart not become filled even with faults?"—may this unbearable arrow of Hari’s message from the wives of Vraja pierce your heart. 375.
Of the Blue One:
(SKM 1.62.1) May the sands of the Kālindī, the evening breezes, and the lovely rays of the moon not fail to remove my fever; why then do they instead cause it to increase all the more?

As Hari heard the message sent by the women of Vraja within the inner apartments, his sighs spread forth; may those sighs, which shatter the pride of the wives' good fortune, be ever victorious. //376//
Composed by the author of the Pañcatantra.
(SKM 1.62.4, UN 15.164) Śrī-Dvārakeśvara’s words addressed to Mudāmaṇa:
"Do not go"—this is an inauspicious word; O friend, speak with words devoid of affection.
"Stay"—this is lordship; "Do as you have spoken"—this is indifference.
We say, "Ah, friend, we rejoice! This is no mere formality.
You must remember us with respect until the time of our next meeting. (377)
Of Hari.
Having seen his own house and so forth, he spoke these words:
"That house has its walls collapsed; this temple has been made spacious by the sky;
that cow is old; and those elephants are herds of clouds."
"That was the trivial sound of pestles; this is the sweet, melodious song of women! Alas, how strange that this brahmin has been elevated to such a high station! (378) — by someone.

Now, at Kurukṣetra, the activities of the Lord of Śrī Vṛndāvana were indicated by that very [hand] which, resembling a blooming lotus shimmering with a fish, was the occasion for a new manifestation of prosperity.
Closing one eye, Rādhā, filled with joy,
gazed at Kṛṣṇa with that left eye.
Of Hara (the beloved of poetic fancy):
Her eyes, veiled by a flood of tears rising from joy, are unable to see;
her arms, sinking and distressed by trembling, are not capable of embracing his neck.

Speech consists of words and syllables faltering with agitation; the mind is restless with turmoil; indeed, even the union with a beloved, having occurred after a long time, acts like a separation. //380//
Of Śubhra. (Attributed to someone in SKM 2.132.1;
to Śrī-Ḍāmara in Sbhv 2065;
to someone in Smv 54.10) Now, [this verse was spoken] to Kṛṣṇa as he was conciliating him in private.
Why do you lie prostrate at my feet, dejected? For masters are independent;
having delighted in someone for a certain time, what fault is there in that? It is I who have committed the offense here, since my life [exists] only in separation from him.
"Women have their lives centered on their husbands; surely you yourself must be conciliated by me. //381//
Of someone: "He who took her as a maiden is indeed the same bridegroom, and those same nights of the month of Caitra. (Attributed to Bhāvadevī; Srk 643 by Vākkūṭa; Smv 57.14)

Those winds from the Kadamba trees are powerful, fragrant with blossoming Mālatī flowers, and I am that very same person; nevertheless, my heart yearns for that spot on the bank of the Revā, at the foot of a Vetasa tree, for the play of amorous dalliance. (382)
For someone [who has attained this state]: "O companion, this is that beloved Kṛṣṇa met at Kurukṣetra;
I am that Rādhā; and this is the bliss of the union of the two."
Nevertheless, my mind yearns for the forest on the banks of the Yamunā, where He enjoys the fifth note of His sweet flute as He plays within. //383//
Of the collector-general.
(Caitanya-caritāmṛta, 2.1.76) A benedictory verse at the conclusion:
O charming girl, abandon your despondency; here Indra’s thunderbolt trembles violently—let it be cast aside.
"Devote yourself to true being, O lotus-eyed one; honor these venerable ones.

May Hari protect you—he who, hearing from Dhanvantari’s verbal artifice during the ritual of the self-choice marriage that Lakṣmī was being taught [to choose], understood this as a prohibition regarding others and an injunction regarding himself. 384.
To a certain [person] from the South—
[namely] Puṇḍarīka—
to him who is the ornament of the Yadu lineage.
Salutation to Hari, who sports in Vṛndāvana and who ferries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. // 385 //
Of Sarasvatī, who is without delay.
Their armlets flash from the collision with the summit of the whirling, radiant Mount Mandara;
they increase the weight upon the trunk of Indra’s elephant and sever the sprouts of decorative leaf-patterns shimmering on the cheeks of the Daitya lords’ wives.
May the staff-like arms of the enemy of Kaṃsa, which steal away the dense darkness of the Kali age's impurity, protect you! //386//
Of the Lord of Yoga (by some).
Whatever compositions exist here, created by Jayadeva, Bilvamaṅgala, and others—
Of these, the verses have been collected here, excluding the others. //387//
May He, whose essence is the most brilliant rasa,
who is surrounded by the swarms of female bees that protect the families of Gokula,
grant whatever one desires.
A certain tree resembling a young tamāla tree. //388//
Thus ends the *Padyāvalī* compiled by the venerable Rūpa Gosvāmī.
Additional verses:
"I have not performed any virtuous deed; alas, I have committed great evil!"
May my destination be the City of Death; what sort of state shall it be there?
No more wandering through the quarters of the day and night—thereafter, act in such a way that my dwelling may be established upon your very shore.
To the King of the city of Gopāla, who is the receptacle for the nectar of Rādhā’s lips and the glory of the essence of the present age;
Homage to you, the one clad in yellow garments!
